title: What learning from data actually means
story:
There is a real distinction between fitting a curve and learning, and it is not about the size of the model. Fitting is a statement about the points you have. Learning is a claim about points you have not seen, and until somebody says what form that claim takes, it is not a claim at all.

Valiant gave it a form in 1984. The paper regards learning as the acquisition of knowledge in the absence of explicit programming — which is the honest description of the situation, since you reach for this whole family of methods precisely when nobody can write the rule down. What it then shows is that machines can be built to provably learn whole characterisable classes of concepts, deducing the desired program in a feasible, polynomial number of steps. Not "tends to work". Provably, for a stated class.

The shape of the guarantee is in the name: probably approximately correct. Two tolerances, and they are separate. One bounds how wrong the learned rule is allowed to be. The other bounds the probability that the learner fails to stay inside the first bound. You cannot drive either to zero with a finite sample, and you cannot trade one away entirely for the other, so every honest statement about generalisation carries both. This is worth internalising because it is the structure underneath every held-out score you will ever report: a number, and a confidence that the number is roughly right.

The result that gives the framework its teeth came later — a concept class is learnable in this sense exactly when it has finite Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension, shown by Blumer, Ehrenfeucht, Haussler and Warmuth in 1989. Read what that says. Learnability is a property of the set of hypotheses you are searching, not of the algorithm doing the searching or the cleverness of the engineer. A class rich enough to fit anything can be learned from nothing, because fitting everything and learning are opposites: a hypothesis space that can accommodate any labelling of the data tells you nothing when it accommodates yours.

Which reframes what the rest of this track is doing. Every method in it restricts the space of functions in some particular way — a line, a tree of a certain depth, a neighbourhood rule — and the restriction is not a limitation to be apologised for. It is the thing that makes generalisation possible.

problem.name: Generalisation
problem.shape: A rule has to behave correctly on inputs nobody has written down, and nobody can state the rule explicitly.
tell: the specification exists only as examples
performance is being claimed on data not yet seen
the model is chosen by how well it fits what you already have
the hypothesis space has never been described
problem.move: State the claim you are making about unseen data, with both of its tolerances: how wrong the rule may be, and how confident you are that it stays within that. Then describe the class of hypotheses you are searching, because that is what determines whether the claim is supportable at all.
problem.invariant: Learnability is a property of the hypothesis class rather than of the algorithm. A class flexible enough to fit any labelling of the data supports no conclusion when it fits yours.
problem.breaks: The guarantee is with respect to a fixed class and a fixed distribution. Change the distribution the data is drawn from and it says nothing — which is why a model can satisfy every theoretical condition and still fail in production, where the distribution is exactly what changed.

cost.time: restricting the hypothesis class costs accuracy on the training data, which is the visible price of the invisible benefit
cost.beats: memorising the examples, which fits perfectly and predicts nothing, and is what an unrestricted hypothesis class amounts to

worked.problem: What does fitting a curve to points have that deserves to be called learning?
worked.reasoning:
On its own, nothing. Fitting is a statement about the points in front of you, and a sufficiently flexible curve fits any set of points exactly while telling you nothing about the next one. The word only earns its place once a claim about unseen data is attached, and the claim has to have a form.

The form that framework gives it is two-sided. Probably approximately correct: one tolerance on how far the learned rule may be from the target, and a second on the probability that the learner overshoots the first. Both are needed, and neither goes to zero on a finite sample. So the honest output of any learning procedure is not a rule but a rule plus an error bound plus a confidence — which is exactly the structure of a held-out score reported with an interval, and exactly what gets dropped when a single number is quoted.

What makes the claim supportable is the restriction on the hypothesis space. The central result is that a class is learnable precisely when its Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension is finite, which means learnability is a property of the class being searched rather than of the search. That is worth stating carefully, because it is counter-intuitive: the reason you can conclude anything from a fit is that your model was incapable of fitting most of the alternatives. A class that can express every possible labelling of your data explains yours no better than chance.

So the answer I would give is that fitting becomes learning when three things are present: a hypothesis class restricted enough that fitting it is informative, a quantified claim about unseen data carrying both tolerances, and data drawn from the distribution the claim refers to.

And the third is where it usually breaks in practice, because everything above is stated with respect to a fixed distribution. A model can satisfy the whole framework and still fail on deployment, since deployment is where the distribution changes — which is a limitation of the guarantee rather than a failure to have met it.

problem.practice: Take a model you have built and write down its hypothesis class in one sentence — what set of functions could it possibly have expressed. Then ask whether that set could have fitted a random relabelling of your data. If it could, work out what your held-out score is actually evidence for.

beats.broke: You want a program that behaves correctly on inputs nobody has written down, and the ordinary route — stating the rule — is closed, because nobody can state the rule.
beats.fix: Acquire it from examples, and replace the demand for correctness with a guarantee carrying two tolerances: probably, meaning with high confidence, and approximately, meaning within a stated error.
beats.cost: The guarantee concerns a class of hypotheses and a distribution rather than your particular dataset, and neither tolerance reaches zero on a finite sample.

interview.q: What does fitting a curve to points have that deserves to be called learning?
interview.trap: Answering in terms of model size or sophistication. A flexible enough curve fits any points exactly and predicts nothing — it is the restriction on what the model could have fitted that makes a fit informative.
interview.answer:
On its own, nothing. Fitting describes the points in front of you, and a sufficiently flexible curve fits any set of them exactly while saying nothing about the next one. The word earns its place only when a claim about unseen data is attached, and that claim needs a form.

The form is two-sided: probably approximately correct. One tolerance bounds how far the learned rule may sit from the target, and a second bounds the probability of exceeding the first. Neither reaches zero on a finite sample. So the honest output of a learning procedure is a rule together with an error bound and a confidence — which is the structure of a held-out score reported with an interval, and precisely what is lost when a single number is quoted instead.

What makes the claim supportable is the restriction on the hypothesis space. A class is learnable exactly when its Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension is finite, which makes learnability a property of the class being searched rather than of the search. The counter-intuitive consequence is that you can conclude something from a fit because the model was incapable of fitting most of the alternatives: a class that can express every possible labelling of your data explains yours no better than chance.

So fitting becomes learning when three things hold — a hypothesis class restricted enough that fitting it is informative, a quantified claim about unseen data carrying both tolerances, and data drawn from the distribution that claim refers to.

The third is where it breaks in practice. All of this is stated with respect to a fixed distribution, and deployment is where the distribution changes, so a model can satisfy the entire framework and still fail. That is a limitation of the guarantee rather than a failure to have met it.

blueprint:
LEARNING = FITTING + A CLAIM WITH QUANTIFIERS

   fitting     about the points you have
   learning    about the points you do not

   the claim, in two tolerances:

      APPROXIMATELY   how wrong it may be
      PROBABLY        the chance it exceeds that

   neither -> 0 on finite data.
   both are always present, stated or not.

THE RESULT THAT GIVES IT TEETH

   learnable  <=>  finite VC dimension

   learnability is a property of the CLASS,
   not of the algorithm.

THE INVERSION WORTH KEEPING

   a fit is informative because the model COULD
   NOT have fitted the alternatives.

   express everything -> explain nothing.

   so every restriction in this track --
   a line, a bounded tree, a neighbourhood --
   is not a limitation being apologised for.
   it is the MECHANISM.

WHERE THE WHOLE FRAME STOPS

   fixed class, FIXED DISTRIBUTION.

   change the distribution and the guarantee is
   silent. deployment is exactly that change.
takeaway: Fitting is about the points you have and learning is a two-part claim about the points you do not — and the reason a fit supports any claim at all is that the model was restricted enough to have been unable to fit the alternatives.
